title: What is the RFC 9457 "Problem Details" standard for HTTP errors (`Content-Type: application/problem+json` with `type` [a stable URL the client can switch on], `title`, `status`, `detail` [human-readable], `instance`, plus a `traceId`), how does Spring expose it (`ProblemDetail` / `ErrorResponse`), and why prefer it over a hand-rolled error shape (a documented, framework-supported contract)?
shortTitle: What is the RFC 9457 "Problem Details" standard for HTTP errors

s1_definition.profdef: RFC 9457, which obsoletes RFC 7807, defines a standard JSON format for HTTP error responses called Problem Details. The response uses the media type application/problem+json and a defined set of fields: type, a stable URL identifying the problem type that clients can switch on; title, a short human-readable summary; status, the HTTP status code; detail, a human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence; and instance, a URI identifying the specific occurrence. You may add extension members such as a traceId. Spring exposes this through the ProblemDetail class and the ErrorResponse interface.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India agreeing with every partner bank on one standard rejection form. Instead of each department inventing its own error slip, everyone uses the same printed form with the same boxes: a reference code box (type), a one-line reason (title), the official rejection stamp number (status), a detailed explanation box (detail), and a case number for this exact rejection (instance). Because it is a standard form, every partner's software already knows how to read it without a custom manual. That standard form is Problem Details.
s1_definition.oneliner: RFC 9457 Problem Details is the standard application/problem+json error shape — type, title, status, detail, instance, plus extensions — that Spring builds in via ProblemDetail so you do not hand-roll your own.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** RFC 9457, which obsoletes RFC 7807, defines a standard JSON format for HTTP error responses called Problem Details. The response uses the media type application/problem+json and a defined set of fields: type, a stable URL identifying the problem type that clients can switch on; title, a short human-readable summary; status, the HTTP status code; detail, a human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence; and instance, a URI identifying the specific occurrence. You may add extension members such as a traceId. Spring exposes this through the ProblemDetail class and the ErrorResponse interface.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India agreeing with every partner bank on one standard rejection form. Instead of each department inventing its own error slip, everyone uses the same printed form with the same boxes: a reference code box (type), a one-line reason (title), the official rejection stamp number (status), a detailed explanation box (detail), and a case number for this exact rejection (instance). Because it is a standard form, every partner's software already knows how to read it without a custom manual. That standard form is Problem Details.

**One line to remember:** RFC 9457 Problem Details is the standard application/problem+json error shape — type, title, status, detail, instance, plus extensions — that Spring builds in via ProblemDetail so you do not hand-roll your own.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has five microservices, and each one historically returned a different error JSON. The mobile app had five separate error parsers, and every new service meant another parser and another round of documentation. This is exactly what Problem Details fixes, because every service returns the same standard application/problem+json shape, so the app needs one parser.

Problem 2 — The app needs to react differently to different problems, for example offering an add money button only for insufficient funds. If it keyed off the human message, a reword would break it. This is exactly why the type URL exists, a stable identifier the app switches on, so wording can change without breaking logic.

Problem 3 — Support needs to trace a customer's failed transfer to the exact server log. The standard allows extension members, so we add a traceId, and the instance field points to the specific occurrence, giving support a direct link.

We will build a transfer service that returns RFC 9457 Problem Details using Spring's ProblemDetail, with a stable type URL per problem, a title, a status, a detail, an instance, and a traceId extension. The demo triggers an insufficient funds problem and a not found problem, showing the standard shape and the application/problem+json content type.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/problem-details-service-1.0.0.jar

# 422 — RFC 9457 Problem Details (Content-Type: application/problem+json)
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"from":"CUR3001","to":"SAV2001","amount":900000"}'
# HTTP/1.1 422
# Content-Type: application/problem+json
# {"type":"https://api.nbi.in/problems/insufficient-funds","title":"Insufficient funds",
#  "status":422,"detail":"Balance 250000.00 is less than requested 900000",
#  "instance":"/api/v1/transfers/...","traceId":"...","balance":250000.00,"requested":900000}

# 404 — account not found Problem Details
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV9999","to":"SAV2001","amount":100"}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a POST transferring 900000 from Priya, who has only 250000, and a POST from a non-existent account.

Step 1: The over-balance POST reaches the controller, which calls the service. The service compares Priya's balance of 250000 to the requested 900000, finds it short, and throws InsufficientFundsException carrying both numbers.

Step 2: The exception bubbles to the ProblemExceptionHandler. It builds a ProblemDetail with status 422 and a human detail. It sets the stable type URL for insufficient funds, the title, an instance URI for this occurrence, and extension members traceId, balance, and requested.

Step 3: Spring serialises the ProblemDetail and sets the content type to application/problem+json automatically. The client receives the standard shape. It switches on the type URL, recognises insufficient funds, and shows an add money button, regardless of the wording in detail.

Step 4: The missing-account POST throws AccountNotFoundException, mapped to a ProblemDetail with status 404 and the account-not-found type URL. The client switches on that type and shows an account not found screen. Both responses share the identical standard shape, so the app uses one parser.

Step 5: Support takes the traceId from the customer's screen and finds the exact server log, because the traceId extension and the instance URI tie the response to the occurrence.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 22:20:00 WARN  POST /transfers over-balance -> 422 application/problem+json
{"type":"https://api.nbi.in/problems/insufficient-funds","title":"Insufficient funds","status":422,
 "detail":"Balance 250000.00 is less than requested 900000","instance":"/api/v1/transfers/...",
 "traceId":"a1b2c3","balance":250000.00,"requested":900000}
2026-10-25 22:20:01 WARN  POST /transfers SAV9999 -> 404 application/problem+json
{"type":"https://api.nbi.in/problems/account-not-found","title":"Account not found","status":404,...}
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — RFC 9457 ProblemDetail ═══

  ┌─ Fields ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  type     stable URL → CLIENT SWITCHES ON THIS           │
  │  title    short human summary (per type)                │
  │  status   HTTP status repeated in body                  │
  │  detail   human explanation for this occurrence         │
  │  instance URI of this specific occurrence               │
  │  +extensions: traceId, balance, requested, ...          │
  │  media type: application/problem+json                   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   ProblemExceptionHandler     │  @RestControllerAdvice
  │  + insufficient() → Problem   │  422
  │  + notFound() → ProblemDetail │  404
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ builds
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   ProblemDetail (Spring)      │  ◆ framework class
  │  type/title/status/detail     │
  │  instance + properties map    │
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────
  1. service throws InsufficientFundsException(250000, 900000)
  2.   → handler.insufficient()
  3.     ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(422, detail)
  4.     setType/ setTitle/ setInstance/ setProperty(traceId)
  5.   → Spring → application/problem+json body
  Contract: type is stable forever ; detail/title may change
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
RFC 9457, which replaces RFC 7807, is the standard format for HTTP error responses, called Problem Details. The response uses the media type application/problem+json and a defined set of fields: type, which is a stable URL identifying the kind of problem and is the field clients switch on; title, a short human summary; status, the HTTP status repeated in the body; detail, a human explanation specific to this occurrence; and instance, a URI identifying this particular occurrence. You can add extension members, and I always add a traceId.

Spring supports this natively through the ProblemDetail class and the ErrorResponse interface. I build a ProblemDetail with forStatusAndDetail, set the stable type URL, the title, the instance, and extension properties like traceId, and return it directly from an exception handler. Spring then sets the content type to application/problem+json automatically, and with the problemdetails flag enabled, even Spring's own built-in exceptions produce problem documents, so the whole API is consistent.

The reason I prefer it over a hand-rolled error shape is that it is a documented, framework-supported contract. At National Bank of India we had five microservices, each with its own error JSON, so the mobile app carried five separate parsers and every new service meant more bespoke documentation. Adopting Problem Details meant every service returned the same standard shape, the app used one parser, and new engineers already understood it because it is an IETF standard with library support across languages.

The detail I stress most is that the type URL must be stable and is what clients switch on, never the title or the detail, because those are human text that can be reworded or localised. The type URL does not even have to resolve to a live page, though we make it a documentation link, but once published it must never change, because it is part of the API contract exactly like the endpoint URLs. That stability is what let our app reliably show an add money button for the insufficient-funds type while we freely improved the human wording, and it is why I reach for Problem Details rather than inventing my own error format.
